name: Sumer
capital: Uruk, Ur, Lagash and other city-states
summary: The first urban civilisation of southern Mesopotamia, made up of rival city-states. It produced the earliest known writing (cuneiform, c. 3200 BCE).

knownFor.label: Cuneiform writing
knownFor.note: The earliest known writing, pressed into clay with a reed.

knownFor.label: The wheel
knownFor.note: Early wheeled vehicles appear in Mesopotamia.

knownFor.label: Epic of Gilgamesh
knownFor.note: Among the earliest great works of literature.

location.value: Southern Mesopotamia (now south-central Iraq), between the lower Tigris and Euphrates rivers.

terrain.value: A flat, marshy river plain that needed irrigation canals for farming. Few stones, metals or timber.

climate.value: Hot and dry. Agriculture depended on river water.

resources.value: Fertile irrigated soil for barley, wheat and dates, plus fish and clay (for bricks and tablets). Metals, stone and timber had to be imported.

disasters.value: River floods (echoed in the Sumerian flood story). Soil salinisation from irrigation slowly reduced harvests.

population.value: Perhaps 0.8–1.5 million people at its height (estimates vary).

urbanisation.value: The world’s first cities. Uruk may have reached 50,000–80,000 people. About 33 cities, including Eridu, Ur, Uruk, Lagash, Nippur and Kish.

disease.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

migration.value: Akkadian-speaking Semites and later Amorites moved in and eventually replaced Sumerian as the spoken language (around 2000 BCE).

economicBase.value: Irrigated agriculture. Surplus grain made the first cities possible, with temples and palaces managing storage.

tradeRoutes.value: Imported obsidian (Anatolia), lapis lazuli (Afghanistan) and cedar (Lebanon). Traded with Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha (probably the Indus Valley).

moneyAndTax.value: Barley and silver by weight were used to measure value. Temple and palace accounts were kept on clay tablets, the origin of writing.

inequality.value: Kings and temple elites, free citizens, and slaves.

governmentType.value: Independent city-states, each ruled by a king (lugal or ensi) linked to its patron god, sometimes united under one dominant city.

keyRulers.value: Enmebaragesi of Kish (the earliest king confirmed by archaeology). Gilgamesh of Uruk (possibly historical). Gudea of Lagash. Ur-Nammu and Shulgi of the Third Dynasty of Ur (c. 2112–2004 BCE).

succession.value: Mostly hereditary dynasties within each city. The Sumerian King List mixes history and legend.

institutions.value: Temple and palace administration, scribes, and the Code of Ur-Nammu, one of the oldest known law codes.

stability.value: Frequent wars between city-states, such as Lagash against Umma over water and land.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between temple priests and kings, and between rival city dynasties.

armyAndTech.value: Infantry phalanxes with copper weapons, and battle wagons pulled by donkeys (shown on the Standard of Ur).

majorWars.value: City-state wars. Conquest by Sargon of Akkad (c. 2334 BCE), invasion by the Gutians, and the Elamite sack of Ur (c. 2004 BCE).

territoryChange.value: Absorbed into the Akkadian Empire, briefly revived under Ur III, then taken over by Amorite kingdoms such as Babylon.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: Elam, Akkad, the Gutians and the Amorites, and each other.

inventions.value: Cuneiform writing (texts c. 3350–2500 BCE), the potter’s wheel, a base-60 number system (still used for time and angles), and the arch.

scienceEducation.value: Scribal schools (edubba). Mathematics and astronomy. Literacy was limited to scribes.

openness.value: Trade spread Sumerian writing and ideas across the Near East.

religion.value: Polytheism with city patron gods (An, Enlil, Enki, Inanna, Utu). Ziggurat temples.

languageWriting.value: Sumerian, a language isolate, written in cuneiform on clay. It survived as a sacred and scholarly language for 2,000 years.

artsArchitecture.value: Ziggurats, the Standard of Ur, the Lyres of Ur, and the Epic of Gilgamesh, among the oldest literature.

socialStructure.value: King, priests and nobles, free farmers and craftsmen, and slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: The Sumerians called their land Kengir and themselves the “black-headed people”.

neighbours.value: Elam, Akkad, Dilmun (Bahrain), Magan (Oman) and Meluhha (Indus).

ideasReligions.value: Writing, law, mathematics and religious myths were passed on to Babylon, Assyria and later cultures.

colonisation.value: Uruk-period trading outposts spread into Syria and Anatolia.

riseSignals.value: Irrigation surpluses, city growth, writing for administration, and long-distance trade.

peakPeriod.value: The Early Dynastic period (c. 2900–2334 BCE), and a revival under the Third Dynasty of Ur.

declineSignals.value: Soil salinisation (population may have fallen by nearly three-fifths, 2100–1700 BCE), invasions, and the rise of Akkadian and Amorite speakers.

outcome.value: Transformation. The Sumerian states were absorbed into Akkadian and then Babylonian kingdoms, and Sumerian culture lived on through them.

sources.value: Cuneiform tablets (hundreds of thousands survive) and archaeology at Ur, Uruk and elsewhere. Checked against Wikipedia on 6 Nov 2026. See also Crawford (2004).

overallCertainty.value: Moderate. Dates are approximate (Wikipedia gives c. 3300–1900 BCE; settlement from about 5500 BCE). Early kings may be legendary, and population is estimated.
